newsitem.title: USA: Sun not yet setting on hot BP shares.
newsitem.headline: Sun not yet setting on hot BP shares.

text.p: British Petroleum Co Plc, continuing to benefit from high oil prices and restructuring, saw its American Depositary Shares (ADS) hit an all-time high Monday, and the stock is still hot, analysts said.

"It's a consequence of the company's restructuring over the past few years," said James Falvey, an analyst with Smith Barney in Boston, adding that yield-conscious investors are likely to be attracted by BP's aggressive dividend growth.
The ADS were trading Monday on the New York Stock Exchange at 135-3/4, up by $3 on the day and by 33 percent in 1996.

"BP has traded at a discount to the other international oil companies for no good reason," said Steven Pfeifer, analyst at PaineWebber in New York, noting he has a target ADS price of price of $140. Twelve ordinary shares on the International Stock Exchange in London equal one NYSE ADS.
Analysts said that while higher oil prices will fuel solid fourth quarter earnings for BP, restructuring efforts have insured BP's profitability even with oil prices much lower.
Crude oil prices settled Friday on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) at $24.17 a barrel, 24 cents lower on the day but $5.60 higher than a year ago.

An official at BP's U.S. unit in Cleveland said the company's internal projections hold that even with NYMEX crude prices at $17 to $19 a barrel ($16-$18 IPE), BP's exploration and production (E&P) activity would still be profitable.

Analysts, who were bullish on the E&P sector as a whole, said one of BP's distinguishing traits among majors is its replacement of oil and gas reserves at the relatively high annual rate of eight to 10 percent.
They noted that while 40 percent of the company's production is now in the Alaskan North Slope, operations in Colombia and in the North Sea look likely to grow briskly.
Growing with equal briskness is the company's dividend, which BP has steadily increased over the last four years since dramatically cutting it in half in 1992, analysts said.

In London, the dividend on ordinary shares is more than restored from pre-1992 levels at an all time high of five pence, though the dividend on the ADS on the New York Stock Exchange is lagging due largely to a less favorable dollar-to-British Pound exchange rate.

Exchange rates also figure highly in the fact that ADS growth of 30 percent in the U.S. this year has outpaced the 25 percent value growth of ordinary shares in London, where they were 5-1/2 pence higher Monday at 675-1/2 pence.
The BP official said the ADS make up around 18 percent of BP's total equity float.
"The dividend growth has been staggering in the last four years," said PaineWebber's Pfeifer, noting that over the next couple of years BP is expected to pile up $3 billion in cash.
The BP official in Cleveland said about half of that cash will likely go back to investors and the other half will be earmarked for investment in certain capital projects.

He did not say whether that distribution would come in the form of a special dividend or more increases to the underlying common stock dividend, but analysts said more increases to the underlying dividend were the more likely scenario.
Analysts also applauded the company's restructuring efforts, particularly its downstream refining and marketing partnership in Europe with U.S. major Mobil Corp, which was launched early in 1996.
They said that venture is now on the verge of reaping benefits.
"When you pull all the factors together, there's a good reason for BP to outperform the market," another analyst said.
-- Oliver Ludwig, New York Energy Desk +1 212 859 1620
